```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
knitr::opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)

# Numbers in the text: fixed decimals and a real minus sign.
num <- function(x, digits = 2) sub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
```

```{r plot-style, include=FALSE}
par(las = 1, bty = "o")    # horizontal axis numbers, full box around the plot
```

This set covers sections 7 to 10. Questions 1 to 5 use the same data; question 6 uses data from a follow-up experiment. Some questions ask you to fit a model in R: run the code yourself. Its output is printed below the code, so you can check that you get the same.

Whenever you interpret a number, say whether it describes these fish (the sample) or trout in general (the population).

## The Data

A hatchery raises juvenile trout to restock a river where the wild population has declined. Fish that are larger when they are released survive better in the river, so the hatchery wants them to grow well. It compared three diets. Each fish was raised alone in its own tank for 12 weeks, in cold (10 °C) or warm (14 °C) water. The file `trout.csv`, in the `data` folder of section 10, has one row for each fish that survived the trial. The data are simulated, with numbers in a realistic range.

| Column       | Meaning                                                          |
|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `fish`       | Fish number                                                      |
| `diet`       | Diet: 1 = commercial pellets, 2 = insect meal, 3 = plant-based   |
| `water`      | Water temperature: `cold` (10 °C) or `warm` (14 °C)              |
| `start_mass` | Mass at the start of the trial (g)                               |
| `oxygen`     | Dissolved oxygen in the tank on day 1 of the trial (% saturation) |
| `final_mass` | Mass at the end of the trial (g)                                 |

```{r data, echo = TRUE}
trout <- read.csv("data/trout.csv")
head(trout)
```

## Question 1: Final Mass and Starting Mass

Fit a model with starting mass as the only predictor:

```{r q1-fit, echo = TRUE}
fit1 <- lm(final_mass ~ start_mass, data = trout)
summary(fit1)
```

The data, with the fitted line:

```{r q1-plot}
plot(trout$start_mass, trout$final_mass, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "starting mass (g)", ylab = "final mass (g)")
abline(fit1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

**(1a)** Write down the model that R fitted, as an equation with the estimated values filled in.

**(1b)** In words, and with units, what does the coefficient of `start_mass` say about trout? Be explicit about whether your statement(s) are about the sample or about the population.

**(1c)** The intercept is `r round(coef(fit1)[["(Intercept)"]], 1)` g. Which trout does the model make this prediction for, and how does that trout compare with the fish in the data?

**(1d)** A colleague points at R² = `r round(summary(fit1)$r.squared, 2)` and concludes that starting mass hardly matters for how big a trout gets. How much does starting mass matter? Use the numbers in the output.

**(1e)** Use the model you wrote down in (1a). Between which final masses does it predict that 95% of trout starting at 20 g will end up? Show how you got the numbers.

## Question 2: A Second Predictor

Add oxygen to the model from question 1:

```{r q2-both, echo = TRUE}
fit2 <- lm(final_mass ~ start_mass + oxygen, data = trout)
summary(fit2)
```

For comparison, a model with oxygen as the only predictor:

```{r q2-oxygen, echo = TRUE}
fit_oxygen <- lm(final_mass ~ oxygen, data = trout)
summary(fit_oxygen)
```

The data from question 1, with each fish coloured by the oxygen in its tank on day 1:

```{r q2-plot}
oxygen_bins <- cut(trout$oxygen, breaks = c(-Inf, 80, 85, 90, Inf), right = FALSE,
                   labels = c("under 80", "80-84", "85-89", "90 or more"))
oxygen_cols <- c("#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b")    # light = little oxygen, dark = much
plot(trout$start_mass, trout$final_mass, pch = 19, cex = 1.2, col = oxygen_cols[oxygen_bins],
     xlab = "starting mass (g)", ylab = "final mass (g)")
legend("topleft", title = "oxygen (%)", legend = levels(oxygen_bins),
       col = oxygen_cols, pch = 19, pt.cex = 1.2, bty = "n")
```

The correlations between the three variables:

```{r q2-cor, echo = TRUE}
round(cor(trout[, c("start_mass", "oxygen", "final_mass")]), 2)
```

**(2a)** The coefficient of `start_mass` went from `r num(coef(fit1)[["start_mass"]])` in `fit1` to `r num(coef(fit2)[["start_mass"]])` in `fit2`. The coefficient of `oxygen` went from `r num(coef(fit_oxygen)[["oxygen"]])` in `fit_oxygen` to `r num(coef(fit2)[["oxygen"]])` in `fit2`. Why did each coefficient change as it did? Use the plot.

**(2b)** A colleague fitted only `fit_oxygen` and concluded that more oxygen makes trout grow less. What can you conclude about oxygen? Be explicit about whether your statement(s) are about the sample or about the population.

## Question 3: Confidence Intervals

The 95% confidence intervals for the coefficients of the three models:

```{r q3-ci, echo = TRUE}
confint(fit1)
confint(fit2)
confint(fit_oxygen)
```

```{r q3-numbers}
ci1 <- round(confint(fit1)["start_mass", ], 2)
```

**(3a)** Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the coefficient of `start_mass` in `fit1` yourself, from the estimate and the standard error in the output of question 1. Show your steps, and check your answer against `confint(fit1)`.

**(3b)** The interval for `start_mass` in `fit1` runs from `r ci1[1]` to `r ci1[2]`. Which of these statements are correct? Explain each answer.

1. There is a 95% probability that the true slope lies between `r ci1[1]` and `r ci1[2]`.
2. If the trial were repeated many times with new trout, and an interval calculated in the same way each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true slope.
3. In 95% of the trout in this trial, each extra gram of starting mass added between `r ci1[1]` and `r ci1[2]` g of final mass.
4. If the trial were repeated with new trout, the new estimate of the slope would lie between `r ci1[1]` and `r ci1[2]` with a probability of 95%.

**(3c)** Suppose the hatchery had raised four times as many trout. Roughly how wide would the interval for `start_mass` in `fit1` be? Explain.

**(3d)** The data are simulated, so we know the population values of the $\beta$s: the values in the model the data were simulated from. In that model, $\beta_\mathrm{start} = 2$: each extra gram of starting mass adds 2 g of final mass. And $\beta_\mathrm{oxygen} = 0$: oxygen has no effect on final mass. Which of the intervals for `start_mass` and `oxygen` above contain these values? Explain what you find.

## Question 4: Diet

Diet is stored in the data as 1, 2 and 3. The mean final mass of the fish on each diet:

```{r q4-means}
diet_names <- c("commercial pellets", "insect meal", "plant-based")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Code = 1:3, Diet = diet_names,
                        `Mean final mass (g)` = tapply(trout$final_mass, trout$diet, mean),
                        check.names = FALSE),
             digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, align = "clr")
```

Two models with diet as the only predictor. In the first, diet goes in as it is stored. In the second, it goes in as a factor, with the codes replaced by the names of the feeds:

```{r q4-fits, echo = TRUE}
fit_codes <- lm(final_mass ~ diet, data = trout)
summary(fit_codes)

trout$feed <- factor(trout$diet, levels = 1:3, labels = c("pellet", "insect", "plant"))
fit_diet <- lm(final_mass ~ feed, data = trout)
summary(fit_diet)
```

**(4a)** Write down both models as equations. For each diet, what mean final mass does each model give?

**(4b)** How much does diet matter for final mass, according to each model? Explain the difference, using the diet means above.

**(4c)** The last line of `summary(fit_diet)` reports an $F$-test. Which hypothesis does it test, and what do you conclude? Be explicit about whether your statement(s) are about the sample or about the population.

**(4d)** Suppose the hatchery had coded the diets differently: 1 = commercial pellets, 2 = plant-based, 3 = insect meal. What would change in `fit_codes`, and what in `fit_diet`? You can answer without fitting anything. To check your answer in R, `trout$diet2 <- c(1, 3, 2)[trout$diet]` gives the new codes.

## Question 5: The Plant-Based Feed

The hatchery wants to know how the plant-based feed (diet 3) compares with the commercial pellets (diet 1). The mean starting and final mass of the fish on each diet:

```{r q5-means}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Code = 1:3, Diet = diet_names,
                        `Mean starting mass (g)` = tapply(trout$start_mass, trout$diet, mean),
                        `Mean final mass (g)` = tapply(trout$final_mass, trout$diet, mean),
                        check.names = FALSE),
             digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, align = "clrr")
```

The diet model from question 4, `fit_diet`, and the same model with starting mass added:

```{r q5-fits, echo = TRUE}
fit_diet_start <- lm(final_mass ~ feed + start_mass, data = trout)
summary(fit_diet_start)
```

```{r q5-ci, echo = TRUE}
confint(fit_diet)
confint(fit_diet_start)
```

```{r q5-numbers}
plant <- "feedplant"
est_a <- coef(fit_diet)[[plant]]
est_b <- coef(fit_diet_start)[[plant]]
ci_a <- confint(fit_diet)[plant, ]
ci_b <- confint(fit_diet_start)[plant, ]
```

**(5a)** Based on `fit_diet` alone, what would you tell the hatchery about the plant-based feed compared with the pellets?

**(5b)** From `fit_diet` to `fit_diet_start`, which adds starting mass, the estimate for the plant-based feed moved from `r num(est_a)` to `r num(est_b)` g, and its 95% confidence interval changed from `r num(ci_a[1])` to `r num(ci_a[2])` g into `r num(ci_b[1])` to `r num(ci_b[2])` g. Explain both changes.

**(5c)** The hatchery's question is only about the feeds. Why does it still make sense to include starting mass in the model? Using `fit_diet_start`, what would you now tell the hatchery? Be explicit about whether your statement(s) are about the sample or about the population.

**(5d)** The data are simulated, so we know the population value of the $\beta$ of the plant-based feed: its value in the model the data were simulated from. In that model, $\beta_\mathrm{plant} = -8$: the plant-based feed gives 8 g less final mass than the pellets. Do the intervals for the plant-based feed in `fit_diet` and in `fit_diet_start` contain this value? What does that tell you about `fit_diet`?

**(5e)** Would you add any other variable from the data to `fit_diet_start`? Why, or why not?

## Question 6: A Follow-Up Experiment

After the first trial, the hatchery considers saving money on aeration. Before it does, it runs an experiment. Fish of about 20 g were selected and assigned at random to one of the three feeds and to high (95%) or low (60%) oxygen saturation, 20 fish for each combination. All tanks were kept at 12 °C. After 12 weeks, each fish was weighed. The file `trout_experiment.csv` is in the same folder as `trout.csv`.

```{r q6-data, echo = TRUE}
experiment <- read.csv("data/trout_experiment.csv")
experiment$feed <- factor(experiment$diet, levels = 1:3, labels = c("pellet", "insect", "plant"))
head(experiment)
```

The mean final mass for each combination of feed and oxygen:

```{r q6-means}
cell_means <- tapply(experiment$final_mass, list(experiment$diet, experiment$oxygen), mean)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Code = 1:3, Feed = diet_names,
                        `High oxygen (95%)` = cell_means[, "high"],
                        `Low oxygen (60%)` = cell_means[, "low"],
                        check.names = FALSE),
             digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, align = "clrr")
```

Two models: one without and one with an interaction between feed and oxygen.

```{r q6-fits, echo = TRUE}
fit_add <- lm(final_mass ~ feed + oxygen, data = experiment)
summary(fit_add)

fit_int <- lm(final_mass ~ feed * oxygen, data = experiment)
summary(fit_int)
```

What each model fits. The lines join the fitted means of each feed; the open circles are the means in the table above:

```{r q6-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.2}
feed_cols <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")
feed_pch <- c(16, 17, 15)
plot_fit <- function(model, title) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.8, 2.2), ylim = c(40, 90), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "oxygen", ylab = "final mass (g)", main = title)
  axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("high (95%)", "low (60%)"))
  abline(h = axTicks(2), v = 1:2, col = "grey88")    # light grid, drawn before the data
  for (d in 1:3) {
    fitted_means <- predict(model, newdata = data.frame(feed = levels(experiment$feed)[d], oxygen = c("high", "low")))
    lines(1:2, fitted_means, type = "o", pch = feed_pch[d], col = feed_cols[d], lwd = 2)
    points(1:2, cell_means[d, ], col = feed_cols[d], cex = 2)
  }
  legend("topright", legend = diet_names, col = feed_cols, pch = feed_pch, lwd = 2,
         bg = "white", box.col = "white", inset = 0.02)    # white box, above the data, keeps the grid out of the legend
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_fit(fit_add, "Without interaction (fit_add)")
plot_fit(fit_int, "With interaction (fit_int)")
```

**(6a)** `fit_add` has four coefficients and `fit_int` has six. Using the plot, explain what the two extra coefficients allow the model to do.

**(6b)** The coefficient of `oxygenlow` is `r num(coef(fit_add)[["oxygenlow"]])` in `fit_add` and `r num(coef(fit_int)[["oxygenlow"]])` in `fit_int`. What does each of these numbers mean?

**(6c)** In `summary(fit_int)`, the coefficient `feedinsect:oxygenlow` has $p$ = `r num(summary(fit_int)$coefficients["feedinsect:oxygenlow", 4], 4)`, and `feedplant:oxygenlow` has $p$ = `r num(summary(fit_int)$coefficients["feedplant:oxygenlow", 4], 2)`. Which hypothesis does each $p$-value test, and what do you conclude? Be explicit about whether your statement(s) are about the sample or about the population.

**(6d)** According to each model, how much final mass would the hatchery lose per fish by lowering oxygen from 95% to 60%? What would you report to the hatchery about the benefit of aeration based on `fit_add`, and what based on `fit_int`?

**(6e)** How does this experiment fit with what you concluded about oxygen in question 2?
